widget.prompt: Maggie walks two trail legs, first 18 m then 24 m, and says the whole trip totals 42 m. Does that check out?

options.label: Yes — 18 + 24 is exactly 42, more than either leg
options.feedback: Correct — a real total must exceed both single legs, and 18 + 24 does equal 42 m exactly.

options.label: No — two trail legs can never be added together
options.feedback: Legs walked one after another do add their full distances; that is exactly how a trail total forms.

options.label: No — 42 m seems too large for two short legs
options.feedback: A total bigger than either single part is expected, not suspicious — that is what joining two legs produces.

options.label: Reasonable only if a ruler re-measures the trail
options.feedback: Sense-checking needs no ruler here — comparing the total to its parts already confirms 42 m.

widget.prompt: Maggie joins a 26 cm strip and a 15 cm strip, then writes 24 cm as the total. Does that make sense?

options.label: No — 24 cm is smaller than the 26 cm strip
options.feedback: Correct — joining 26 with anything more lands past 26; a 24 cm total contradicts its own first strip.

options.label: No — the total must be exactly 31 cm
options.feedback: 26 + 15 makes 41, not 31 — a ten went missing. And even without the sum, 24 cannot beat 26.

options.label: Yes — 24 cm is bigger than the 15 cm strip
options.feedback: Beating one strip is not enough — a joined total must pass BOTH strips, and 24 trails 26.

options.label: Yes — a written total can come out any size
options.feedback: Totals obey their parts: 26 + 15 must land past 26, never below it.
